paras: The shooting of Hampton Price was the fatal shooting of a Black man described as a "negro conjurer and so called doctor" by Oliver, the town sergeant of Franklin, Southampton County, Virginia, in December 1881. According to the reports, Price struck the officer with a black-jack when the sergeant pressed him to return fifty cents paid for a charm, and Oliver shot him in the back as he fled. Oliver was charged with the shooting, and Virginia papers took note when both witnesses for the Commonwealth died within days, leaving the prosecution without evidence.

According to a dispatch first printed by the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer on December 19, Price "had become hard up in his own neighborhood" and came to Franklin professing to be a conjurer and doctor. The Norfolk version of the dispatch said he came "to try his conjuring scheme on the ignorant negroes there." An elderly Black man "in well to do circumstances" paid him half a dollar for a charm that was supposed to lead its owner to a mine of coined gold. When no mine turned up, the man asked for his money back, and Price refused.

The town sergeant, named as Oliver in the Norfolk dispatch, then renewed the demand, on the 17th according to a Dallas telegram. Price again refused and, by these accounts, struck the officer with a black-jack he carried, dealing Oliver "four or five blows over the head." Oliver then drew his pistol and shot Price in the back as he was running.

Reports from Petersburg later in the month described the encounter as an arrest rather than a dispute over money. The Richmond Dispatch's correspondent wrote that Oliver was struck twice on the head with a "black-jack" by the man he was trying to arrest, while the Petersburg Index-Appeal said he was felled to the ground with a slung-shot. Neither account mentioned the shot in the back, saying only that Oliver fired and mortally wounded him.

Oliver was "charged with shooting a negro whom he was about to arrest," the Dispatch's Petersburg correspondent wrote on December 24. Only two people had seen the shooting, both of them Black, and the Commonwealth summoned both as witnesses. Three days after the shooting one was killed by a fall from his horse, and a few days later the other died of malarial fever before the case was called in court. As the correspondent put it, "the Commonwealth is thus left without any evidence"; no report of an inquest, trial or verdict appears in the coverage.

The shooting reached papers outside Virginia as a short wire item: the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran it on December 19 as "A Negro Conjurer Mortally Shot," the Dallas Daily Herald included it among its "Latest Telegrams Condensed" on December 20, and the Wilmington Daily Republican printed a Norfolk dispatch headed "A Pretended Conjurer Fatally Shot" on December 21. These items told the story as the end of a swindle, calling the old man Price's "dupe" and "victim," the Dallas paper referring to him as an "old darkey."

Virginia coverage later in the month turned to the case against Oliver. The Richmond Dispatch filed the item under "Litigation Ended by Death" and reminded readers that Oliver "was discharging his duty as an officer." The Petersburg Index-Appeal, reprinted by the Montgomery County Sentinel of Rockville, Maryland, on December 30 under "Some Singular Circumstances," remarked that the case was "not exactly a 'celebrated case'" because the deaths had removed all testimony that might have made it sensational.

Accounts differ on why the sergeant confronted Price: the wire dispatch said he renewed the old man's demand for the money, while the Petersburg reports said he was attempting an arrest. They also differ on the weapon, a black-jack or a slung-shot, and on whether Oliver was struck four or five times or twice. The Norfolk dispatch printed on December 21 placed the shooting "last night," but the story was already in print in Lancaster on December 19, which fits the Dallas telegram's date of the 17th. Every version came from the officer's side or from reports on his prosecution, and no statement by the witnesses was printed before they died.

reader.title: Shooting of Hampton Price
bases: A town sergeant acting in his official capacity shot a Black man who, by the officer-side accounts, struck him while resisting a demand or an arrest; no crowd was involved (A1, A3, A4, A5).
The wire dispatch (A1, A2, A3) and separate Petersburg reports (A4, A5) agree that Town Sergeant Oliver shot and mortally wounded a Black man at Franklin after being struck with a weapon.

accounts.label: Petersburg reports (Richmond Dispatch correspondent; Index-Appeal)
accounts.gist: Oliver was trying to arrest the man in his official capacity, was struck with a black-jack or slung-shot, and fired, mortally wounding his assailant; both witnesses later died.

framing.detail: Headlines 'A Negro Conjurer Mortally Shot' and 'A Pretended Conjurer Fatally Shot' cast Price as a swindler of 'his dupe' and gave the officer's version without comment.
The Richmond Dispatch's Petersburg correspondent wrote that Oliver 'was discharging his duty as an officer' and treated the witness deaths as litigation 'ended by death'.
The Index-Appeal, under 'Some Singular Circumstances', dwelt on the oddity of both witnesses dying within ten days.
